prize_parts.citation: For showing how collateral constraints and asset prices amplify and propagate shocks, creating the theory of credit cycles.

statement.case_for: My preferred part is unchanged: a single B002 award to Kiyotaki and Moore. Kiyotaki-Moore (1997) is a compact general-equilibrium mechanism. Borrowing limits tied to collateral values feed back on asset prices, so temporary shocks become persistent and amplified. The idea is conceptually original and now sits inside macro-finance, quantitative macro and central-bank modelling, with almost three decades of follow-up. Credit is clean because the founding paper has two authors. The exchange sharpened my reasoning but did not change the configuration. On the chair's overlap question, I apply one principle to every candidate: adjacency to an earlier prize is neither a merit criterion nor a reason to reject a candidate. It matters only if the earlier prize rewarded the same discovery. Applied consistently, B002 versus 2022 (banks, runs and intermediation), B025 versus 2008 (scale economies and variety), and B050 and B021 versus 2024 (institutions and prosperity) are each a question of whether the mechanism is distinct. For B002 I judge that it is, because the collateral-and-asset-price feedback is a different mechanism from runs and intermediation. I hold this as a judgment, not a settled fact. On the chair's evidence question, I do not have in the supplied record anything that would let me quantify collateral amplification. I recall studies using variation in collateral values to explain firm investment, but I cannot verify them here and I do not change any ranking on that basis. The change from round 1 is limited to my alternatives. I drop B021 and add B012 next to B025. After the exchange I weigh the unsettled persistence and shift-share debate and the bundling of tasks and trade shocks more heavily in B021. I also take more seriously the argument that B012's method has stayed standard through three decades of robustness debates.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises may be read as having covered neighbouring ground. Direct empirical identification of the size of collateral amplification is also weaker than the theory's influence. A Kiyotaki-Moore award leaves the financial-accelerator and intermediary strand (Gertler, Gilchrist) unrecognised, which some colleagues see as part of the same body of work. A two-name citation is therefore narrower than the full financial-frictions literature. Finally, a single mechanism award gives up the breadth that a two-part configuration spanning methods and mechanisms might offer.

responses.point: Teorell is the only member proposing two parts: Kiyotaki and Moore for B002 and Pakes alone for B012. He uses the three-person cap to drop Gertler and credit one name for B012, and he admits that Pakes alone omits Berry and Levinsohn from BLP.
responses.response: I agree with his two-name B002 and I am glad the exchange moved him off Gertler. I would not support the second part as proposed. My objection is mainly attributional, not thematic. The demand-estimation breakthrough is Berry-Levinsohn-Pakes. Crediting Pakes alone for it would misdescribe where the discovery came from, and he himself records this as a real loss that the cap forces. A configuration that fits only by cutting names whose contribution is central is worse than a clean single part. I do not object to pairing a mechanism with a method as such. If the Committee wanted a two-part prize, I would need a B012 citation anchored on a defensible laureate set, and under the three-person cap that set does not fit beside Kiyotaki and Moore. So B002 alone stays my preference. I treat B012 as a serious alternative and not as a second part.

responses.point: In reply to my round 1 worry about attribution spread and structural-assumption robustness, Strömberg argues that identification and computational debates have run for three decades and the method stayed standard, which signals maturity. He would anchor the award on the demand-estimation core with Pakes and not claim all of new empirical IO.
responses.response: I accept the maturity argument. A method that stays standard through decades of critique has passed a real test, and that is why B012 now moves into my alternatives. I also accept that anchoring the citation on the demand-estimation core with Pakes's dynamic work answers part of my attribution worry. Two concerns remain for me. The first is that Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin are left out, and several colleagues, including Hjalmarsson and Andersson, say a narrow citation does not fully remove that cost. The second is how much weight a measurement framework should receive against a conceptual mechanism. I hold that weighing loosely. My preference for B002 rests on cleaner credit and on the conceptual originality of the mechanism, not on a view that methods are less valuable. If the Committee settled the Bresnahan question and wrote the citation narrowly, I would not call B012 an unreasonable choice.

responses.point: Hassler, who ranks B002 first, keeps Gertler as a third name. He separates Gertler's later intermediary-based quantitative work with Kiyotaki and Karadi from Bernanke's 2022 recognition, and he accepts the two-name version as a fallback.
responses.response: I take the separation seriously. The intermediary-based models are a distinct strand from the runs-and-banks analysis of 2022, and they build on the collateral mechanism. My objection is to the unit of credit, not to Gertler's merit. The three-name version asks the citation to cover collateral-driven credit cycles and also the broader finding that financial frictions propagate fluctuations. Gertler's most influential work, as I read it, sits in the accelerator lineage and the New Keynesian ballot, so his credit is divided and the citation becomes harder to bound. Answering the chair's question directly, I do not oppose a three-name version in every form. If the Committee wanted a broader financial-frictions citation, Gertler's case should be made on his own contribution. I would still prefer the narrower prize with a clearly bounded origin, and I am glad Hassler accepts it as an acceptable fallback. Since he is the chair and a frequent co-author of mine, I note that I am answering on the merits and not out of proximity.

responses.point: Dreber ranks B025 first on the strength of more than twenty years of firm-level confirmation. She places B002 second, citing its clean two-author origin, but sees thinner empirical confirmation of collateral amplification. She concedes that omitting Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum is a genuine attribution risk.
responses.response: Her empirical point is the sharpest challenge to my preference and I do not dismiss it. The firm-level evidence for exporter selection is richer than the evidence on the size of collateral amplification, and I keep that in my case against. I weigh it differently for two reasons. First, the question for B002 is whether the mechanism became the working framework of a field and of policy modelling, and I think it did, partly because the 2008 crisis tested its relevance. Second, the attribution gap she concedes for B025 is a cost of the same kind as the thinner empirical confirmation of B002, and the gap is a real one. For that reason I keep B025 as my first alternative. I also agree with her that the Krugman 2008 overlap is a question of whether the mechanism is distinct, and I think the selection and reallocation mechanism is. That is how I would apply the same principle to B002 and the 2022 prize.

uncertainties: How much of the collateral-amplification mechanism the Committee regards as already covered by the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises.
How strongly the direct empirical evidence supports quantitatively large collateral amplification, which I cannot assess from the supplied record.
Whether the Committee prefers a broader financial-frictions citation that includes Gertler, and whether his credit is better placed here or with the New Keynesian ballot.
How the Committee weighs a conceptual mechanism against a measurement framework such as B012, and whether the omission of Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin undermines a three-name BLP award.
Whether the omission of Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum is serious enough to prevent a Helpman-Melitz award.
I rely on the shortlist text and colleagues' stated recollections and have not independently verified citation counts, prior-prize scope or relative credit.
statement.conflict_note: I am a frequent co-author of Per Krusell and a co-author of John Hassler (chair), and an IIES colleague of both. Both prefer B002, and the chair's version adds Gertler. I disclose this and do not adjudicate it. I have a long-running collaboration with Peter Klenow (also with Aghion, Bergeaud and Li). Klenow is a credited name on B017, which is in neither my preferred configuration nor my alternatives. The supplied profile shows no apparent connection to Kiyotaki, Moore, Gertler, Gilchrist, Pakes, Berry, Levinsohn, Melitz, Helpman or Redding. The profile gives weak evidence that I may have helped draft the 2025 Scientific Background, which does not bear on this slate.
